instructions: The night before, or at least 5 hours ahead, trim both ends off the 4 cucumbers.

Sprinkle 1/2 tsp of the salt over a cutting board. Roll the cucumbers in it, pressing down with your palm, for about 30 seconds each, until they turn a darker green and a little green juice comes out.
Rinse the salt off under cold water and pat the cucumbers dry with a paper towel.
Cut the kombu into thin strips with kitchen scissors.
Pour 1 1/4 cups cold water into a large zip-top bag and add the remaining 2 tsp salt. Seal it and squish the bag until the salt dissolves.
Add the kombu strips and the cucumbers to the bag. Press out the air, seal it and lay it flat in a dish in the fridge overnight, up to 2 days. Turn the bag over once if you're passing the fridge.
When you're ready to serve, lift the cucumbers out of the brine. Push a wooden chopstick or a thick skewer into one end of each, about halfway up.
Serve them cold, one cucumber each.
advance_prep_notes: Salt the cucumbers and put them in the kombu brine the night before, or at least 5 hours ahead.
method_notes: All three versions rub whole cucumbers with salt, rinse them and chill them in a brine with strips of kombu. RecipeTin Japan (the lead) keeps the brine to water, salt and kombu and leaves the cucumbers whole overnight; Just One Cookbook adds rice vinegar, sugar, soy sauce and dried chili, pickles them for 5 to 6 hours and pushes a chopstick in just before serving the festival way; La Fuji Mama slices them into a vinegar brine in a jar. This follows RecipeTin Japan's brine and borrows Just One Cookbook's chopstick, and kombu (not bonito) keeps it vegan. No version read had 20 or more ratings, so this falls back to RecipeTin Eats, the trusted cook for this cuisine, whose Japanese site has the version used here.
